Summary (auto-gen, rough):
Quick technical triage for accuracy regressions after quantization (INT8/AWQ/FP8 variants). Focus areas: layerwise sensitivity, KV cache warmup noise, batching interplay with KV cache and latency SLO, onprem/VPC constraints for benchmarking, and a bisect plan for isolating regression layer(s).

Topics:
- Observed behavior: 1-3% semantic drift on long-context QA and instruction-following samples after AWQ conversion; some hallucination spikes on multi-turn flows.
- Hypotheses: layer mismatch during quantize (outlier activations), stochastic rounding artifacts in FP8 path, KV cache stale keys due to batching condensation, and misaligned warmup paths in onprem runtime.
- Plan: layerwise quant sensitivity sweep, offline bisect with mixed-precision rollbacks, heatmap artifact, targeted canary on Dedicated, fallback gating in runtime.

Transcript body (timestamps rough, transcription imperfect):
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about an hour, want to go deep on the quant regression you reported. can each of you give a quick context?
[00:12] Sofia: yeah thanks maya. we're seeing subtle but real drops in accuracy after we move to awq-int8; it's mainly multi-turn clinical QA prompts, and it's weird because latency improved but the clinical correctness drops on a few categories.
[00:28] Mei: yeah i'll add — when we run long context chains the model starts to hallucinate discharge instructions, which is obviously bad. not every prompt, but a cluster of prompts.
[00:38] Liam: ok that's helpful, thanks. Arjun / Tom, what's your bench and network for the onprem runs? are you running with the same kv cache warmup as cloud?
[00:47] Tom: we're using 8x A100-s XM I think, custom runtime build; we did a quick port of your runtime but used our local kernel set, so there might be small exec differences. kv warmup is shorter than your hosted defaults — we trimmed warmup for latency.
[01:03] Noah: small note — shorter warmup can change the kv sticky behavior, which may surface as stale kv entries and degrade coherence in multi-turn.
[01:12] Mei: interesting, we did reduce prefix warmup because tokens cost for us, but maybe that caused more cold hits.
[01:20] Liam: right, so hypothesis one: kv cache warmup reduction increases early-turn error rate; hypothesis two: AWQ quantization introduces layerwise scale mismatch on certain attentions leading to semantic drift. both could be in play.
[01:34] Maya: can we prioritize an experiment plan? what do you need us to run, and we'll run here on hosted too to compare.
[01:41] Arjun: we want a concise bisect plan. also security — Leah — will need to see what data leaves and if we can keep bench artifacts inside our VPC.
[01:50] Leah: yes please. we need assurance on no PII exfiltration and we'll want an onprem bench option. also SOC2 docs.
[01:58] Priya: we'll share SOC2 + security whitepaper after the call, and we can sign an NDA if needed for sample prompts.
[02:07] Mei: to add more detail: failing prompts tend to be templates with long patient histories and nested bullet lists, so KV/key alignment for long sequences probably relevant.
[02:20] Liam: ok let's talk quant specifics — you tested AWQ int8 and an FP8 run?
[02:26] Mei: yes — AWQ gave the best latency but had regressions; FP8 kept accuracy better but latency was worse and memory usage jumped. GPTQ try was mixed and took a long time to compile.
[02:39] Liam: typical tradeoff. AWQ sometimes introduces small bias in outlier layers if activation distributions are heavy-tailed. FP8 stochastic rounding helps but is noisy and more memory. GPTQ can preserve accuracy but has compat issues with certain kernels.
[02:54] Tom: kernel set differences could explain why onprem AWQ looks worse than hosted — our CUDA kernels are slightly older and some fused ops differ.
[03:03] Liam: good point — we should match kernel versions. we'll provide a minimal container spec for bench to reduce that variable.
[03:11] [03:11] Timestamp glitch, speaker overlaps
[03:15] Sofia: can you explain how layerwise sensitivity sweep would work? what metrics will you look at?
[03:21] Liam: sure. we'll quantize one layer at a time (or groups) and run evaluation suite that includes: per-layer perplexity delta, semantic similarity (embedding-based) against golden outputs, and a small safety/regression test set. we'll produce a heatmap that highlights layers where INT8/AWQ causes biggest drift.
[03:38] Mei: do you have tooling to do the sweep without full model export each time? that was a blocker for us.
[03:44] Liam: yes — our runtime supports on-the-fly layer swapping in our dev harness; we can avoid full export by loading float model and patching layer kernels to quantized variants. this reduces iteration time.
[03:55] Arjun: great, speed matters. how long would a full sweep take for our 34B model?
[04:01] Liam: estimate 6-10 hours for full per-layer sweep with our harness on 8 GPUs, shorter if we parallelize per-layer groups. we'll provide a prioritized list so you can run the highest-risk layers first.
[04:13] Maya: let's also discuss kv cache interplay — how batching and coalescing affect kv timeliness.
[04:19] Noah: batching changes the order and timing of requests hitting the KV manager; if a batch collapses many small requests, some tokens that should be in cache become delayed, warming different keys at different times. that creates transient incoherence.
[04:35] Tom: that matches our observation — under peak QPS, the clinical multi-turn flows diverged after the second or third turn.
[04:43] Liam: mitigation — we can try sticky batch hints for long sessions, or increase prefix persistence for sessions flagged as multi-turn; both are config knobs we can test.
[04:55] Mei: what's the runtime cost of sticky sessions? does latency go up?
[04:59] Noah: slight memory overhead per session for longer persistence, and some scheduling complexity. but it stabilizes semantics for long flows.
[05:07] Sofia: can we instrument the warmup hits so we know when a session hits cold vs hot KV?
[05:12] Liam: yes — we'll add a KV heatmap and a warmup hit rate metric. those will be part of the bench artifact.
[05:20] Maya: ok next, fallback and rollout strategy — assume we identify a suspect layer, what's the safe way to deploy?
[05:26] Liam: we recommend canary gating with the ability to patch specific layers back to float for canary traffic. rollout steps: 1) run internal canary on Dedicated 2) small percent production canary with quality eval hooks 3) automatic rollback on quality delta > threshold. we can automate layer patch gates in the runtime.
[05:43] Arjun: sounds good. how does that interact with VPC/onprem where we don't control runtime easily?
[05:49] Liam: for Private/onprem, we'd deliver a hotfix container and a patch script that does the layer swap; for customers that can't take runtime patches fast, we provide a fallback to serve request to hosted variant under policy (routing), subject to compliance approval.
[06:05] Leah: routing sensitive data offprem is a blocker. we need to keep PII inside VPC unless redwood's paper says otherwise.
[06:12] Priya: understood — most customers prefer onprem fallback, we can prioritize a private canary process for you.
[06:18] Mei: about bisect — can you outline the bisect steps?
[06:21] Liam: quick outline: 1) reproduce failure baseline on float and quant locally 2) run binary search replacing blocks of layers between float and quant to find smallest set that reproduces regression 3) once identified, run micro-eval on that layer with more data 4) try mixed-precision on that layer (fp16 or fp32) and see if it resolves.
[06:39] Sofia: do you plan to test stochastic rounding or different zero-point handling?
[06:43] Liam: yes. we'll test stochastic rounding for FP8 paths and alternative calibration methods for AWQ (per-channel vs per-tensor). we'll also try layerwise bias correction.
[06:53] Mei: what about kv cache order sensitivity — can we simulate different batching/coalescing to see if it's a factor?
[06:58] Liam: absolutely, we'll run bench scenarios with: small single-session batches, aggressive coalesced batches, and sticky session mode. capture turn-by-turn logits and KL divergence to track drift.
[07:12] Tom: kernel mismatch again — if we see a quant-only problem on your hosted runtime but not ours, it could be fused-op difference. how deep do you want kernel parity?
[07:20] Maya: we'll provide container spec + nccl/cuda versions; ideally you run bench with our provided container. if that's impossible, note the kernel diffs and we'll triage.
[07:29] Arjun: security question — Mei will share prompts, but can we hash them and only send hashes to Redwood? we need to be careful.
[07:35] Leah: yes hashing is preferred; we can provide hashed ids and run bench locally with results shared as metrics.
[07:41] Priya: ok we can accept hashed sets for initial investigation, later we'll sign NDA to share raw samples if needed.
[07:48] Liam: for instrumentation we'll need example outputs too — hashes + metrics sometimes insufficient to diagnose subtle semantic drift, but we'll start with hashes and deltas.
[07:58] Mei: timeline?
[08:00] Liam: we'll start layerwise sweep immediately after the call; expect initial heatmap by 2027-06-22. if that pins a layer, we'll propose a mixed-precision rollout for a canary within 48 hours of identification.
[08:10] Maya: and we'll share security docs today.
